newsitem.title: USA: Fatter wallets may mean Q4 U.S. consumer comeback.
newsitem.headline: Fatter wallets may mean Q4 U.S. consumer comeback.

text.p: A sluggish pace of consumer spending growth during the summer months could give way to a healthy fourth quarter bounceback, economists predicted this week.
Just how healthy a rebound remains unclear at this point, but early fundamental and anecdotal signs suggest a robust pace of consumer activity may round out the year.
Rising incomes, record stock market levels, lofty consumer sentiment measures and a slew of new homes in need of new furnishings could add up to good news for retailers in the months ahead.
Last Friday's retail sales figures showed sharp downward revisions in August but unexpectedly strong September numbers, suggesting consumers may already have begun emptying their fatter wallets.
Overall retail sales rose by a robust 0.7 percent in September while sales excluding automobiles advanced at a healthy 0.4 percent pace.
"It does give you the sense that the quarter ended on a firm note and has some fairly good momentum going into the fourth quarter," said Doug Schindewolf, money market economist at Smith Barney Inc.

Schindewolf, who is looking for consumption growth between 3.0 and 3.5 percent in the fourth quarter versus estimated gains of about one percent in the third, predicts the faster pace of growth will prompt the Federal Reserve to tighten rates before the end of the year.
Economists say continuing strength in the labor market, which has so far failed to translate into higher spending levels, is the key to any consumer rebound.
"If people have jobs and income they will probably spend it," said Donald Straszheim, chief economist at Merrill Lynch.

Straszheim said the 40,000 decline in September non-farm payrolls cannot be taken at face value, but warned that he does expect employment growth to slow, denting consumer spending in the holiday months.

But the current combination of lower unemployment, higher wages and greater wealth through record stock price gains has other market observers convinced that a robust holiday shopping season is upon us.

"We're more optimistic on the consumer and less concerned about the story the consumer may be overstretched primarily because we're focused on the combination of income gains and wealth effect," said Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at consulting firm I.D.E.A. Inc.

Economists said existing home sales demand through August suggests there will be a need to furnish houses in the coming months. And with the Dow Industrials closing over 6,000 for the first time ever on Monday, households that invest are clearly seeing their net worth rise.

On the other hand, consumer installment credit grew by a paltry $3.3 billion in August, underscoring the weakness in consumer spending during the summer months and suggesting shoppers may be overstretched.

"You have to ask yourself if that's the beginning of a new trend ... or if the consumer is more likely to come out spending in the fourth quarter culminating in a strong Christmas -- that is our bias." said Stiles.

Data from large U.S. chain stores last week showed mixed sales in September, but suggested that chilly fall weather had lifted business across the board at the tail end of the month, bolstering hopes for a strong holiday season.
If confidence measures are any indication, then consumers should be spending at far higher rates heading into the holidays.

The University of Michigan's sentiment index showed considerable strength in its preliminary October reading last week, while the Conference Board's survey of confidence for September also hinted that consumers may be poised for a breakout.
Consumers are "quite optimistic about the next six months," the Conference Board said. "With consumers in high spirits, the outlook for holiday spending appears to be bright."
